title: Geraint the Bookworm's Bumpy Beginning
markdown:
Felix the ferret was pleased. His button collection, shiny, sorted by colour, was the best in the burrow. Every button belonged. He liked neat. He also knew a little silliness could improve a Tuesday, and that too much silliness made a mess with its own postcode.

The Sunny Meadow School library was usually quiet and cozy. Sunlight on tall windows, rows of books. Mr. Alder loved quiet and neat shelves, eyes kind and crinkled, voice gentle. Felix traced titles with a curious paw. Ivy the deer read about starry skies and quiet forests.

One Tuesday Mr. Alder stood at the desk, hands a little trembly. “A new campaign: Return Books on Time.” He held a slightly droopy banner. “And our new mascot: Geraint the Bookworm.”

From behind a velvet curtain Geraint waddled out — floppy brown cloth, huge round glasses that looked permanently surprised, antennae dangling almost to the floor. Very big. A bit clumsy. Fabric feet went swish-swish on the wood.

Felix’s whiskers twitched. Geraint swayed like a tree trying to wave. “A giant sleepy caterpillar who forgot how to stand.” Ivy blinked. “Very large for the aisles. He might bump.”

“Nonsense,” Mr. Alder puffed, tweed straining. “Cuddly. He will remind everyone.” Geraint took a clumsy step. Giant feet caught the rug. He tipped. A display of new books tumbled. Soft thuds. Felix, eager when things got exciting, scurried over and tangled in the trailing legs. Ivy picked up a book about badger homes and shelved it. The campaign had begun with a wobble.

Then the fun, if you asked Felix. Geraint knocked a tower of encyclopedias — thump. His floppy head stuck in fiction, glasses crooked. One afternoon he slid across the polish with a surprising rush; children gasped and giggled. Felix appointed himself co-pilot and cheered every lurch. “The most exciting thing to happen to this library.”

Ivy watched Mr. Alder’s brow furrow by degrees. A hand over neatly combed hair after each adventure. A quiet sigh that did not belong in a good campaign.

The busiest chaos was story time, the hour Mr. Alder loved most, when even fidgets sat. Geraint was meant to listen in the corner like a kindly sofa. A brave knight excited him into a grand gesture. The huge fabric arm swept a shelf of picture books into a fluffy paper landscape, thump-thump-thump, a geography of covers. Children watched the accident instead of the knight. One asked if the bookworm was the dragon. Felix, to his later shame, almost cheered. Mr. Alder looked at the mess, at the drooping costume head, at the audience that had changed the subject. Shoulders slumped. The sparkle went tired. He closed the knight mid-quest and did not open another page that afternoon.

“This campaign is a disaster.” He whispered it, but the shelves heard. No one was thinking about overdue books. Everyone was talking about the accident-prone bookworm.

At the desk, lamplight long, he felt the library’s quiet thought replaced by a nervous buzz: what would Geraint knock next? Felix saw his part. He had loved the excitement. The silliness had made Mr. Alder unhappy. A stone in the tummy. Not a nice one.

Ivy walked over. “Perhaps he does not need to be quite so enthusiastic. A calmer helper.” Felix, wanting to make it right, scampered beside her. “I can teach careful. A gentle book-helper.”

The next week they held a Book Buddy Parade. Felix guided every step, whispering. Small colourful ribbons on Geraint’s paws: instead of flailing, he carried returns like treasures. He stood still by the desk, glasses gleaming, a friendly calm.

The murmur of readers came back. Mr. Alder’s smile returned, crinkles and all. Late books began to trickle in, a few sheepish faces. More important: the safe quiet, the feeling of a favourite story, had a place to sit again.

Felix logged curtain-waddle / story-time sweep / ribbon parade in the library book, left one encyclopedia stacked a little loosely as a joke he did not repeat, and let Ivy choose the next starry-sky title while Geraint held the returns, proud and still. The mascot, who had started as a bump, had learned how to stand in an aisle.
